did_you_know.text: Isaiah describes Ephraim using images of a crown and a fading flower, linking its pride to drunkenness and a life of pleasure in a fertile valley.
The approaching disaster is described as a fierce storm: hail, a devastating wind, and a mighty flood sweeping over the land.
In contrast to Ephraim’s crown of pride, the Lord is described as a crown of glory and a beautiful diadem for the remnant of his people.
The criticism is not directed only at the people: the chapter explicitly says that both priest and prophet went astray through drunkenness, causing them to err in vision and judgment.
The repeated phrase “command upon command, command upon command; rule upon rule, rule upon rule” describes short, repetitive instructions that the hearers mock instead of accepting.
The prophet presents rest for the weary and refreshment as part of the message that the people refuse to hear.
The rulers of Jerusalem are described as saying that they have made a covenant with death and with Sheol, trusting in lies and falsehood as a shelter from the overwhelming scourge.

In contrast to the shelter of lies, the Lord declares that he is laying in Zion a tested stone, a precious cornerstone and a firm foundation; the verse says that whoever believes will not act hastily.
Justice and righteousness are described as measuring tools: justice as a line and righteousness as a plumb line, while hail and water will expose and sweep away the shelter of falsehood.

The final part of the chapter contains an agricultural parable: a farmer does not plow without stopping, but adapts the plowing, sowing, threshing, and grinding to the types of seeds and the purpose of the work.
